newsitem.title: USA: Another financial scandal rocks troubled Miami.
newsitem.headline: Another financial scandal rocks troubled Miami.

text.p: Another financial scandal has broken over Miami, a city already so mired in corruption that disgusted residents may abolish it as a municipal entity later this year.
The director of Miami's bustling sea port, who was facing questions about the port's finances, abruptly announced his retirement over the weekend, officials said Monday.

Port Director Carmen Lunetta, 67, apparently made the decision after documents obtained by The Miami Herald showed seaport revenues had been spent on Super Bowl tickets, luxury car rentals and campaign contributions, including contributions to current county commissioners.
Lunetta faxed his retirement letter to Dade County Manager Armando Vidal, who had no immediate comment.

"After much thought, deliberation and discussions with my family, I wish to advise you of my decision to retire as Director of the Port of Miami, effective July 31," he said in his resignation letter, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters.

Lunetta, port director for 38 years, said he expected to remain a consultant to the county for six months after his resignation. He was out of town and would not be back until Tuesday, his secretary said.
The Herald did not directly accuse Lunetta of a crime but said he had jurisdiction over the port's budget and directed a contractor to make some of the questionable expenditures.
Lunetta built the facility into a major gateway that bills itself as the world's busiest cruise port and one of the largest container shipping ports.

The port is overseen by Dade County, which believed it to be self-supporting. But a report released under pressure from county commissioners last week revealed the port actually had a $22 million deficit and that taxpayer funds had been used to offset port losses for several years.
The revelations prompted Commissioner Miriam Alonso and Commissioner Jimmy Morales, who chairs the commission's finance committee, to call for a complete investigation of the seaport's books.
The port's woes came to light as Miami voters prepared for a Sept. 4 referendum on a proposal to dissolve the city and merge it into the Dade County government.

The city of Miami is only a fragment of the urban sprawl generally known by that name. Most of the greater Miami area is actually run by Dade County authorities or is part of separate cities such as Coral Gables and Miami Beach.
Disgruntled residents forced the referendum after three top city officials resigned to face charges they accepted bribes or solicited kickbacks from city contractors.
After the resignations last fall, an interim city manager discovered that Miami had a $68 million deficit in its $275 million budget for fiscal 1997.

While Dade County remains solvent, its finances have also been under scrutiny. The Securities and Exchange Commission has subpoenaed documents from both the city and the county and is examining their tax-exempt bond issues.

Dade County Commissioner James Burke, meanwhile, has acknowledged he is a target of Operation Greenpalm, an ongoing federal investigation that resulted in indictments against the three city officials. Burke has denied any wrongdoing.
